# Synthetic birth-profile fixtures

**Every profile here is invented.** None describes a real person. This is the only
birth data that development, CI and evaluation are permitted to use.

That rule exists because of the free-tier PII constraint (ADR-004): birth date + birth
time + birth place is, in combination, close to a unique identifier, and free model
tiers may train on their inputs. Synthetic fixtures make "never send real user data to
a free provider" enforceable rather than aspirational.

## Structure

```
charts/
├── profiles.json       the inputs — 30 cases, chosen for edge coverage
└── expected/<id>/      expected_d1.json + expected_dasha.json per case
```

`profiles.json` is GENERATED by `services/astro/scripts/build_profiles.py`. Edit that
script, not the JSON. The reason is `expected_utc_offset_min`: it is an assertion about
tzdata, and the twelve hand-written profiles that preceded this got one wrong — 009
claimed Calcutta was +05:53 in 1901, and tzdata says +05:21 (Madras Mean Time, which
British India ran on from 1870 until IST in 1906). A plausible number, reasoned rather
than looked up, and wrong.

So the offsets come from Python's `zoneinfo` and are asserted in Go against
`time/tzdata` — two independently packaged copies of the tz database that have to
agree.

`expected/` is generated by `services/astro/scripts/generate_golden.py`, which
**refuses to run** unless `services/astro/tests/test_external_reference.py` passes
first. That suite compares the engine against dated astronomical events — equinoxes, the
2020 great conjunction, the 2017 eclipse, Mesha Sankranti, published Saturn transits, a
Mars retrograde season — none of which came from this engine.

**A golden file that encodes your own bug is worse than no test at all** — it makes the
bug permanent. Cross-validate before freezing, and the generator enforces it.

## Why these thirty

Each exists to break a specific assumption.

| ID | Case | What it catches |
|---|---|---|
| 001 | Delhi, 1990, morning | Baseline. Nothing special. |
| 002 | Mumbai, 1985, 00:12 | Date boundary — midnight can land on the wrong Julian day |
| 003 | Kolkata, 1943 | **Wartime DST.** India ran UTC+06:30, not +05:30. |
| 004 | London, 1995 | Non-Indian timezone with its own DST rules |
| 005 | Anchorage, 2000 | Extreme latitude — house systems degenerate near the poles |
| 006 | Quito, 1988 | Equator — the opposite degenerate case |
| 007 | Pune, 1998, time unknown | **Must return null** for ascendant, houses and dashas |
| 008 | Chennai, 2000-02-29 | Leap day in a century year that *is* a leap year |
| 009 | Kolkata, 1901 | **Pre-IST.** tzdata says Madras Mean Time, +05:21 |
| 010 | Jaipur, 1994 | Ascendant near a sign boundary |
| 011 | Sydney, 1979 | Southern hemisphere + DST |
| 012 | Village, manual coordinates | Coordinates typed rather than chosen |
| 013 | Kathmandu, 1987 | **+05:45.** A quarter-hour offset |
| 014 | Chatham Islands, 2005 | **+13:45.** Quarter-hour offset *and* DST |
| 015 | Tehran, 2005 | +03:30/+04:30 on a Persian-calendar DST schedule |
| 016 | Adelaide, 1995 | +09:30/+10:30, southern-hemisphere DST |
| 017 | Lord Howe Island, 2015 | The world's only **30-minute** DST shift |
| 018 | St John's, 2005 | The only **negative** half-hour offset, −02:30 |
| 019 | Apia, 2010 | Samoa east of the date line, −11:00 |
| 020 | Apia, 2012 | The **same place** after skipping 30 Dec 2011: +13:00 |
| 021 | Kiritimati, 2000 | +14:00, the largest offset in use |
| 022 | Kolkata, 1900 | The de421 kernel's lower edge |
| 023 | Tokyo, 2050 | The kernel's upper edge — dashas project decades out |
| 024 | Delhi, 2001 | Moon at sidereal 359.9999° — the 359→0 wrap, found by search |
| 025 | Delhi, 1996 | Mercury 0.6 arcmin into Capricorn — a planet on a cusp |
| 026 | Tromsø, 1985 | 69.6°N in December: polar night |
| 027 | Invercargill, 1999 | 46.4°S, the southern mirror |
| 028 | Kolkata, 1942 | Brackets 003 from **below** — before wartime DST |
| 029 | Kolkata, 1945 | Brackets 003 from **above** — after it ended |
| 030 | Reykjavík, 1988 | Unknown time, 21° west of a UTC zone meridian |

Fixtures 003, 009, 019 and 020 are the ones most likely to be got wrong, and the reason
the Phase 2 spec insists timezone resolution uses a real tzdata lookup rather than a
fixed offset. 028 and 029 exist because 003 alone would pass for an implementation that
always returned +06:30 for Kolkata.
